Good afternoon, Mayor and members of the Council.
For those who have not met or spoken to me before, my name is Emily Ruck.
I'm the Artistic Director of the Roxy Regional Theater and have been since August of 2023.
I wanted to speak to you in person tonight since I know your inboxes are flooded
and I wanted to make sure that what I had to say was heard,
mainly because I want to set the record straight on a few things
and address a couple of concerns that you all brought up last week,
as well as that I've seen repeated online.
First and foremost, I think it is important to reiterate,
and I would hope that you would all be more active in helping our residents understand this,
that property taxes cannot be used to pay for the project of the Performing Arts Center.
That is a repeated concern I'm seeing on the internet,
and understandably so as a resident and homeowner myself.
I certainly don't want higher property taxes,
but that's not at play here.
And without quelling those concerns, you are allowing a false narrative to run rampant.
I want to give you some details on where the Roxy Regional Theater currently stands financially
and its profitability since, even though we are a separate entity from the Act Authority,
this continues to be brought up and questioned.
Of course, the Roxy has dealt with its share of financial shortcomings in the past.
When I took over running the organization in April of 23,
the Roxy had less than three weeks of payroll for a nine-person staff,
and we were able to maintain a track record of every show making back its investment,
and then some, until recently.
Twenty-two productions in a row, almost three full seasons,
until the final show, season 43, which was presented in our temporary space.
I knew moving into the temporary space would cause a loss eventually,
as our capacity to make a profit off productions has been more than cut in half,
and costs are not going down.
That's simple math.
Of course, the Roxy has received support from the city through the years.
However, the claim seen online that the city has poured millions into the Roxy is barely true.
Going back 11 years, not counting the sale of the building,
before the Roxy Regional Theater was moved under the umbrella of the Act Authority
and taken out of the city's annual budget,
the city has given the Roxy a total of $822,028 in funding assistance.
Throw in the sale of the building,
which the city would be refunded for as part of the interlocal agreement,
the total comes to $1,632,028 over 11 years.
That is approximately the amount some other non-profits receive from the city
in only a time period of roughly a year and a half.
I've also repeatedly heard,
why can't we just rip off a section of F&M Arena to perform?
The answer is, we have.
We rented the arena this past March for our daytime performances of Junie B,
and we did the due diligence of serving,
the teachers after the fact, on their and the students' experiences.
The overwhelming majority responded that if we were to continue partnering
with the arena for these performances, they would not bring their students.
How can we serve our school system and students,
and those of the surrounding counties,
if they won't come to the productions because of where it's at?
We can't.
The arena was not designed or built for live theater.
It is not a viable option for theatrical performances,
and some of our most important audiences who are vital to our mission as an organization,
have voiced that to us.
It has been said, the project is too expensive,
and we need to go back to the table.
The truth is, we never left the table.
The ask was made to cut $15 million off the project,
a mere two to three months before construction was scheduled to begin.
Pencils were resharpened, adjustments were made, and cuts were made.
If this is too expensive in the long run,
then I don't see how other possible ventures,
such as the idea of an amusement park or water park,
which are guaranteed to be just as, if not more expensive,
as well as putting a strain on local resources,
are a smart idea when they would only provide seasonal income and jobs.
A performing arts center operates and contributes to the economy year-round,
and by nature of programming, constantly provides something new for the community and visitors.
I understand the desire for pledges to be obtained before commitment is given.
To that, I simply ask this.
What is the incentive for a company or individual to pledge several millions of dollars to a project that seems to keep stalling?
F&M didn't come on board for the Orinda until construction was underway.
Mion Enterprises didn't step in for the garage until construction was underway.
The City and Council did commit to this both with the purchase of the building
and again with the creation of the Act Authority.
A vote for those two decisions was a pledge, one that has not yet seen fruition.
I'm not saying it's entirely impossible to get those pledges.
I'm just asking for the difficulty in that ask to be recognized
and not thrown around like it's as easy as finding a vape shop or car wash in Clarksville.
The comment was made last week that we would be leaving the debt
to the next generation to solve.
And that is simply not true.
The responsibility of keeping this burden off of the City's shoulders falls squarely
on Cameron as the Executive Director of the Act,
but also on myself as the Artistic Director of the resident company and anchor tenant of the Pack.
That's five minutes.
Thank you.
